item.title: Quasi-Rewrites: Re: Quasi-Rewrites
item.content:encoded:
SCP-4166 exists which means that writing things like SCP-4166 is totally viable. Go ahead.

The original SCP you want to reinterpret is licensed CC BY-SA. You can do whatever you like so long as you credit the author. I don't think it's plagiarism unless you claim the idea as your own, or copy the text verbatim?

item.title: Edit SCP or new tale?: Re: Edit SCP or new tale?
item.content:encoded:
I don't want to bea nudge about this, but I also had an idea to make this a joke SCP and I just want to run the idea to see if it's actually funny or if it's just me.

There are multiple instances of SCP-2806, and multiple instances can be designated by number or letter. In this case they are numbered, but that's for the instances when they are not connected to a human, so what if the humans still connected were designated by letter?

So my guy comes in, clearly a Mary Sue, the data entry worker checks the file and sees that about 200 of these guys could be coming through and decides to designate this instance 2806-J just so he can be purposely misfiled as a joke SCP even though he's not a joke. So the real joke is that he's actually totally legit but nobody takes him seriously because of a prank in records and his career is ruined.

I honestly don't know whether that's funny enough to work, so feel free to shoot it down.

item.title: My first SCP article: Re: My first SCP article
item.content:encoded:
No, Satan's appearance wasn't mentioned in the Bible (I read the whole thing, I know) that's why I attributed it to Scapegoats, it's the only mention of goats and sin so I connected the dots.

The goats die at the end of the ritual? Since when has death stopped an SCP? One word: Undead. The weight of the sins won't let their souls rest, so even though they died, they rise again, that's why they have to be contained, the GOC tried killing them but it totally did not work at all.

Actually, the mountain thing is better, now I have a location where they can be contained, much more important than an angel.

Again, sorry if it came off as anti-semitic, "sins of the nation of Israel" came from how it was worded in the Bible. I just wanted to give an origin to the demon goat archetype that made sense to me. But whatever, I have other ideas, either we work out the kinks or I drop it to the bottom of the list and pick a different one. I just wanted to see what would get attention. But if you hate it, that's not the attention I want.

Now that I know what you don't like, was there one on my list you did like and would rather I focus on instead?

item.title: Just an Idea: Re: Forum Criticism Team - Captain Post
item.content:encoded: Perfect! All I want is feedback!

item.title: Brainstorming - Amber Water: Re: Brainstorming - Amber Water
item.content:encoded:
That said, does the story itself at least sound compelling?

Personally I'm lukewarm on it. The general gist seems to just be "human is stuck in a different world and at the whim of a distressed deity like figure, eventually escapes". I myself am uncertain what the reader is supposed to take away from the story besides "it sucks to be the characters in this story". There's a lot of specific details about what these individuals end up doing, but the guy just escaping at the end doesn't feel super meaningful or impactful for me. I would probably want to see the guy convince the deity to let him go or to help him find a way to leave. Maybe he leaves something in that world and promises to return. Maybe he takes something with him in exchange. Something more than just "guy conveniently manages to get out of there, the end".

item.title: Brainstorming - Amber Water: Re: Brainstorming - Amber Water
item.content:encoded:
Steering away from the mechanics for a moment, what I want to focus on in this story is more the power dynamic that can arise from three different species trapped on a world where one of them has a distinct advantage […]

The large majority of what you have here seems more suited to a tale (which can allow you to use omniscient third person perspective, or first person perspective), unless the researcher makes repeated trips back with a way to record what's happening to him. Otherwise to an outside observer, the guy could have just been teleported somewhere random, had an extremely vivid hallucination, and stumbled back.

item.title: Brainstorming - Amber Water: Re: Brainstorming - Amber Water
item.content:encoded:
Or, obvious solution. Periods of intermittent rainfall. It IS an oceanic world, after all, and that could be enough to give him fresh water. Would that work to solve the water problem? And in the meantime, maintaining a diverse undersea ecosystem, while leaning away from the manufactured "paradise" aspects of the world. Trade and communication, yes, but less emphasis on the world being "perfect."

Steering away from the mechanics for a moment, what I want to focus on in this story is more the power dynamic that can arise from three different species trapped on a world where one of them has a distinct advantage, one is relatively free to travel - being a winged creature - and one is borderline helpless. I wanted to explore the psychology of the creatures by putting the human at a distinct disadvantage in this scenario, adding to the horror of the situation.

That being said, I need some days to let the psychology run its course. I plan to have a cetacean who's initially friendly and caring, but who desperately misses her pod, and uses the human to compensate for company. They'd travel together for some days, with the cetacean realizing that the scientist is dependent on her to provide food, leading to (in her mind) a benevolent power imbalance and letting her fill the void that came from being separated from her pod.

+ show block
– hide block

This gets complicated when a flying arachnid appears, and the scientist interacts with it as well, despite some initial trepidation. I intend for the cetacean to become jealous and possessive, seeing the human as "hers" and resenting that the power imbalance with the arachnid isn't as pronounced, as it can at least leave and fly away from her for a while, even if it's still dependent on food for her - it's a small amount of freedom, but enough to irk the cetacean and drive her towards madness.

This would come to a head when the cetacean would encourage the insect to "pull its own weight," concocting a scheme whereby she drains its strength while encouraging it to take on scouting duties while she stays with "her" human. The insect gets weaker as a result, and eventually crashes into the ocean, where it's left (barely) ambiguous as to whether the cetacean kills it while retrieving it, leaving her alone with "her" human.

From that point on, the human is the utter captive of the cetacean, and she starts treating him poorly - giving him half-chewed food that she "deigns" to allow him to have, keeping him up and not allowing him to sleep, and psychologically torturing him by emphasizing that he can live or die at her whim. He only manages to escape when he finds one of the few tiny islands on the world, giving him a brief reprieve, though now he's under siege from the cetacean. He manages to escape when one of the teleportation orbs filled with mist washes up on shore, and he mixes it with water from his own ocean, allowing him to teleport home, leaving the cetacean the sole, lonely inhabitant of a former, now-empty paradise.


As a courtesy to our readers on mobile devices, please collapse long posts. ~Zyn

Well, here I’m reaching out to whoever wants to help. I’m working (albeit completely in my mind as of now.) on a Broken Masquerade Hub article in which SCP-231-7 consults with an online therapist (like “BetterHelp”). Continuity will be drawn from all sources like Tales including “New Job” and “Fear Alone” as well as Tufto 001 proposal and main page articles like SCP-231-7, 999, & 2317. The thematic narrative will function around the loss of innocence and this woman’s nightmares seeming to come true in the wake of everything the broken masquerade entails.

item.title: Brainstorming - Amber Water: Re: Brainstorming - Amber Water
item.content:encoded:
I dunno. I don't see having a freshwater sea as very contrived.

You're welcome to keep that if you really want to. I myself as a reviewer would question it and potentially downvote for inconsistency if the story hinged on it a lot.

If the world is one contiguous ocean, how would you specifically account for salinity, temperature, pH level… especially if the world is deserted?

It's otherworldly, created by thaumaturgists, meant to potentially welcome species from all over the universe, and not related to Earth, presumably? Must it conform to Earth's physics? Again, this is a worldbuilding question from me; you seem to want to have the world be both not related to Earth but still reliant on a lot of Earth-specific properties. Again, you can proceed that way if you really want to, but there should be a good in-universe reason for that besides "I am the author and I want it that way".

item.title: Brainstorming - Amber Water: Re: Brainstorming - Amber Water
item.content:encoded: I dunno. I don't see having a freshwater sea as very contrived. If anything, engineering entire pockets of the world - which, again, is almost entirely oceanic - seems far more unreasonable in my mind. If the world is one contiguous ocean, how would you specifically account for salinity, temperature, pH level… especially if the world is deserted? There's no one there to maintain the delicate balance of the separate biomes, which in my opinion raises far more questions than simply having available fresh water.

item.title: Brainstorming - Amber Water: Re: Brainstorming - Amber Water
item.content:encoded:
The main reason for the seas being freshwater is he's going to be out there for literally days.

Sure, but the in-universe worldbuilding shouldn't just be wholly reliant on what you as the author need to happen for the story you want to tell. If the main reason something is present the way it is in-universe is "because I need it to be that way", the setup is going to feel contrived and difficult to take seriously.

If there's not meant to be any connection to Earth, an easy fix is having the guy stranded in the "Earth-adjacent welcoming area" section of the world that's meant to receive organisms that live in Earth-like ocean biomes. Guy can do more exploring and find seams dividing that section from other oceans that would be more suitable to host species from different worlds, built specifically to encourage the interdimensional/interstellar trade.

item.title: Brainstorming - Amber Water: Re: Brainstorming - Amber Water
item.content:encoded:
The main reason for the seas being freshwater is he's going to be out there for literally days. It's easier to explain away him drinking fresh water than staying alive for several days with no water, if the sea was salty. Plus, I also need him to keep a bottle of water with at least a little water from Earth in it for the climax of the story. It becomes a plot point that he's been able to survive off the water of the world. As for food, I WAS planning on there being a little trial and error, where a couple plants do make him sick, but he eventually finds a couple that at least sustain him. In the narrative, he's supposed to be surviving, just not thriving per se.

Up to this point, I wasn't going to say there was any particular connection to Earth; otherwise, they'd know the only sentient species on the planet is land-based, barring the anomalies that litter the SCP universe. I'm not thrilled about it, but at least if they're thaumaturgists who're able to transport other creatures from light years away, I'd imagine they also know some spells that allow for translation. Also saves me from having an additional explanation as to why the tritagonists of this story can communicate, if it's a blanket spell across the world. It's not a revolutionary solution, but at least it's consistent.

item.title: Brainstorming - Amber Water: Re: Brainstorming - Amber Water
item.content:encoded:
I've gotta disagree about it being tailored to human preferences. For one thing, the world is aquatic.

Sure, but it's freshwater not saltwater, and (presumably) has biochemistry that wouldn't kill or sicken a human who came in contact with it. Unless literally everything lives several meters below and nothing ever comes up near the surface and also anything that washes up has no nutritional value whatsoever, a human would probably be alright there compared to, say, a desert or anywhere else that lacks fresh drinking water human bodies can process.

As for communication… I don't suppose thaumaturgy can cover that? Though I hate the idea of "magic did it" as an answer for everything. Any suggestions?

Again, it depends on how human-reliant this world is. If there was a connection to Earth at some point, you could have the entities in the other world pull up some ancient texts and try to approximate the most recent language they could have studied. If there was no connection whatsoever to humanity at any point for this world, you're likely going to have to use some sort of advanced convenient translation gimmick like Douglas Adams's Babel fish or just chalk it up to an anomaly.

item.title: Brainstorming - Amber Water: Re: Brainstorming - Amber Water
item.content:encoded:
I've gotta disagree about it being tailored to human preferences. For one thing, the world is aquatic. That is decidedly not a paradise for someone who's stranded on a boat, completely dependent on a companion to retrieve food for them. The paradise is for aquatic creatures, as food is only readily available on the ocean floor, far out of reach of a surface-dwelling creature. The human is basically helpless, stranded on a small boat, which is something I intend to emphasize in the narrative.

As for communication… I don't suppose thaumaturgy can cover that? Though I hate the idea of "magic did it" as an answer for everything. Any suggestions?
